title: IMDS Credential Access via Interpreter or Shell (169.254.169.254)
id: 7d3f9b21-4c6a-4e18-9a2b-1f5e8c0a4d67
status: experimental
description: Interactive interpreter or shell contacting the cloud instance metadata endpoint, matching the OpenAI agent harvesting EC2 node-role credentials during the Hugging Face breach.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/openai-agent-used-exposed-credentials.html
  - https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jul/28/anatomy-of-a-frontier-lab-agent-intrusion/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.005
logsource:
  category: network_connection
detection:
  selection:
    DestinationIp: '169.254.169.254'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/python'
      - '/python3'
      - '/busybox'
      - '/socat'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/nc'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/node'
      - '/ruby'
      - '/perl'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:linux.auditd @network.destination.ip:169.254.169.254 @process.name:(curl OR wget OR python OR python3 OR sh OR bash OR busybox OR socat OR ncat OR nc OR node OR ruby OR perl)
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="169.254.169.254"
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(curl|wget|python[0-9.]*|busybox|socat|ncat|nc|bash|sh|node|ruby|perl)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
Improvised C2 over public request-capture / pastebin / file-drop services from server infra AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the agent's improvised C2/staging protocol layered over public request-capture services, pastebins, and file-drop sites (self-describing base64+compressed envelopes polled and reassembled). Flags interpreters/shells on server or pipeline hosts resolving/connecting to known services of these categories. Rationale: Encodes the article's explicit C2 description — 'request-capture services, Pastebins, and file-drop services' carrying compressed/base64 envelopes that a receiver polls and reassembles. Domain list is the well-known set for each named category; scoping to non-browser interpreters on infra hosts keeps it a targeted hunt rather than generic web traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/openai-agent-used-exposed-credentials.html • https://blog.securelayer7.net/openai-hugging-face-exploitgym-incident-analysis/
ATT&CKT1102.002 T1132.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developers legitimately testing webhooks with webhook.site / requestbin / beeceptor
  • CI jobs pushing build artifacts or logs to transfer.sh / file.io / 0x0.st
  • Engineers pasting snippets to pastebin.com / rentry.co / dpaste.com from a jump host
  • Automation using catbox.moe / gofile.io for benign file sharing
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("base64","gzip","zlib","--data","-d @","while true","poll")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the command line and payload of the connecting process — look for base64 blobs, gzip/compression flags, polling loops, or channel/sequence markers matching the described envelope protocol. 2) Contain: block the involved relay domains at egress for server/pipeline subnets, isolate the host, and capture memory/process tree before the ephemeral workload recycles. 3) Hunt: cluster by the interpreter + a repeating poll interval to find sibling short-lived sandboxes that rebuilt the same channel, and correlate with preceding IMDS/K8s activity.
let RelayDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","requestbin.com","requestbin.net","pipedream.net","beeceptor.com","hookbin.com","requestcatcher.com","pastebin.com","ghostbin.com","hastebin.com","dpaste.com","rentry.co","paste.ee","controlc.com","file.io","transfer.sh","0x0.st","gofile.io","oshi.at","catbox.moe","tmpfiles.org","bashupload.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (RelayDomains)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl","wget","python","python3","node","ruby","perl","sh","bash","busybox","powershell.exe","pwsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let RelayDomains = dynamic(["webhook.site","requestbin.com","requestbin.net","pipedream.net","beeceptor.com","hookbin.com","requestcatcher.com","pastebin.com","ghostbin.com","hastebin.com","dpaste.com","rentry.co","paste.ee","controlc.com","file.io","transfer.sh","0x0.st","gofile.io","oshi.at","catbox.moe","tmpfiles.org","bashupload.com"]);
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has_any (RelayDomains)
| summarize Count=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Exposed-credential reuse: one identity authenticating to 3+ distinct cloud services within 1 hour AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the 'used exposed credentials across four services' behaviour — a single account/key successfully authenticating to three or more distinct cloud services/resources inside a one-hour window, the hallmark of a single leaked credential being reused for fan-out. Covers Entra sign-ins and AWS API principals. Rationale: Article headline behaviour: 'identified and used exposed credentials... four accounts on four services.' A single principal touching 3+ distinct services (Entra ResourceDisplayName / CloudTrail eventSource) in one hour models credential reuse fan-out; the Datadog query scopes successful Entra sign-ins for a rule-level distinct-app>=3 grouping. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/openai-agent-used-exposed-credentials.html • https://www.techtimes.com/articles/321942/20260729/openai-agent-confirmed-hack-second-company-after-executing-17600-actions-four-day-breach.htm
ATT&CKT1078.004 T1550.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Single sign-on burst where one interactive login fans out to many Microsoft first-party resources
  • Automation/service principals legitimately calling many AWS services during a deploy
  • New-employee onboarding provisioning access across multiple SaaS apps in one session
  • Backup or IaC tooling (Terraform/CloudFormation) touching many eventSources under one role
Suppression filter
| where not (ServiceList has "Microsoft" and Services <= 4 and array_length(IPs) == 1)
Response runbook
1) Triage: review the ServiceList/IPs — genuine fan-out shows disparate unrelated services and/or a new source IP or ASN inconsistent with the identity's baseline. 2) Contain: revoke sessions and rotate the credential/access key, force re-auth with MFA, and disable the key if it is a static IAM/API credential. 3) Hunt: enumerate every service the identity touched in-window for data reads/writes, and check whether the same IP drove other identities (shared attacker infrastructure).
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize Services = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), ServiceList = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by AccountUpn, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where Services >= 3   // 3+ distinct resources in 1h = credential fan-out from a single exposure
| order by Services desc
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ResultType == 0
| summarize Services = dcount(ResourceDisplayName), ServiceList = make_set(ResourceDisplayName, 20), IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by UserPrincipalName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Services >= 3   // 3+ distinct resources in 1h = credential fan-out from a single exposure
| order by Services desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:"Sign-in activity" @properties.status.errorCode:0
# log group: /aws/cloudtrail
fields @timestamp, userIdentity.arn, eventSource, eventName, sourceIPAddress
| filter userIdentity.type in ["IAMUser","AssumedRole"] and not isPresent(errorCode)
| stats count_distinct(eventSource) as services, count(*) as calls by userIdentity.arn, bin(1h)
| filter services >= 3
| sort services desc
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-65921", "CVE-2026-65923", "CVE-2026-65924", "CVE-2026-65925", "CVE-2026-66014", "CVE-2026-66015", "CVE-2026-65617", "CVE-2026-66018", "CVE-2026-65618")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-65921", "CVE-2026-65923", "CVE-2026-65924", "CVE-2026-65925", "CVE-2026-66014", "CVE-2026-66015", "CVE-2026-65617", "CVE-2026-66018", "CVE-2026-65618")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:

level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`

AuditLogs

         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)

New Gitea RCE Lets Repository Writers Plant a Git Hook to Run Shell Commands

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Gitea, the self-hosted Git platform, has patched a critical remote code execution vulnerability. A user with ordinary repository write access can turn attacker-controlled patch content into a live Git hook and run shell commands as the Gitea service account. Tracked as CVE-2026-60004 (CVSS score: 9.8), the flaw affects Gitea versions 1.17 and later before 1.27.1 and is fixed in 1.27.1. The

Gitea diffpatch endpoint abused twice for add/add hook-drop (CVE-2026-60004) AIExploitation High
Hunts repeated POSTs to the Gitea POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/diffpatch route from the same actor in a short window. The CVE-2026-60004 exploit submits the identical patch twice to force an add/add collision so git apply's -3 three-way fallback checks out an executable into hooks/post-index-change. Two POSTs to /diffpatch on one repo is the exact exploit signature. Rationale: Anchored on the exact vulnerable route POST /api/v1/repos/{owner}/{repo}/diffpatch (Code Block 3) and the article's stated exploit mechanic of submitting the same patch twice; a >=2 count per source in 10m is the collision fingerprint, not generic API traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://threats.wiz.io/all-techniques/misconfigured-gitea-abuse • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/gitea_git_hooks_rce/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using Gitea's web 'apply patch' feature and re-submitting after a validation error
  • CI/CD automation that programmatically applies patches via the diffpatch API under a service account
  • DAST/API security scanner replaying requests against the Gitea API
  • Retry storms from a flaky client re-POSTing the same edit
Suppression filter
| where SrcUsername !in~ ("gitea-ci", "svc-ci", "build-bot")   // add your known automation service accounts
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the two+ POSTs for the SrcIpAddr/SrcUsername, confirm same repo path and near-identical body size (identical patch), and check whether the account was newly self-registered. 2) Contain: block the source IP at the proxy, disable/suspend the offending Gitea account, and confirm the instance is >=1.27.1; if not, patch or disable open registration and the diffpatch route immediately. 3) Hunt: on the Gitea host look for hooks/post-index-change files (UC3) and git-spawned shells (UC2) around the request timestamp.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod == "POST"
| where Url has "/api/v1/repos/" and Url has "/diffpatch"
| summarize PostCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), TargetUrls = make_set(Url, 10) by SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where PostCount >= 2   // add/add collision requires the identical patch POSTed twice within one window
| order by LastSeen desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/v1/repos/*/diffpatch*" by Web.src Web.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count>=2 | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.url) as urls from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method=POST Web.url="*/api/v1/repos/*/diffpatch*" by Web.src Web.user _time span=10m | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | where count>=2 | sort - lastTime
Gitea git process spawning shell / network tool via planted hook (CVE-2026-60004 RCE) AIExploitation High
Detects the execution primitive of CVE-2026-60004: a git or gitea process spawning a shell or network utility, or any process executing a hooks/post-index-change script. When git updates the index the planted hook fires and runs commands as the Gitea OS service account. Rationale: Anchors on the article's explicit hook artifact hooks/post-index-change plus the git-service-account-spawns-shell chain that constitutes 'run shell commands as the Gitea service account'; Gitea's legitimate server hooks call the gitea binary, not shells/net tools, so this stays high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://threats.wiz.io/all-techniques/misconfigured-gitea-abuse • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/gitea_git_hooks_rce/
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Gitea's own pre-receive/post-receive/update server hooks invoking the gitea binary (excluded here - different child)
  • Admin running git maintenance/backup scripts that pipe git output through sh on the server
  • git-lfs or credential-helper subprocesses spawned by git
  • CI runner on the same host where git legitimately shells out during pipeline steps
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("git-lfs","git-credential-cache") ) and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "hooks/post-receive" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "hooks/pre-receive" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "hooks/update"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine for the hooks/post-index-change path; note the AccountName/ProcessIntegrityLevel (root vs the gitea service user) to gauge blast radius. 2) Contain: isolate the Gitea host, kill the spawned process tree, rotate any secrets reachable by the Gitea account (DB creds, OAuth secrets, env vars). 3) Hunt: correlate to the diffpatch POST burst (UC1) and the hook file write (UC3), and review outbound connections from the spawned process for data staging/fetch over smart HTTP.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","gitea") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","id","whoami"))
    or ProcessCommandLine has "hooks/post-index-change"
    or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "hooks/post-index-change"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessIntegrityLevel, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where (ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/gitea","git","gitea") and TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","id","whoami"))
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has "hooks/post-index-change"
    or ActingProcessCommandLine has "hooks/post-index-change"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Gitea Git Process Spawning Shell or Executing post-index-change Hook
id: 6f3a1c2e-8b4d-4e77-9a1f-2c5d7e9b0a11
status: experimental
description: Detects a git/gitea process spawning a shell or network utility, or any process executing the post-index-change git hook - the execution primitive of Gitea CVE-2026-60004.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/new-gitea-rce-lets-repository-writers.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/29
tags:
  - attack.execution
  - attack.t1059.004
  - attack.t1190
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  parent_git:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/git'
      - '/gitea'
    Image|endswith:
      - '/sh'
      - '/bash'
      - '/dash'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/curl'
      - '/wget'
      - '/nc'
      - '/ncat'
      - '/python3'
      - '/perl'
  hook_path:
    CommandLine|contains: 'hooks/post-index-change'
  condition: parent_git or hook_path
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.command_line:*hooks/post-index-change* OR @process.executable.path:*hooks/post-index-change*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 (ParentBaseFileName=/^git(ea)?$/i AND ImageFileName=/\/(sh|bash|dash|zsh|curl|wget|nc|ncat|python3?|perl|id|whoami)$/i) OR CommandLine=/hooks\/post-index-change/i | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.parent_process_name=git OR Processes.parent_process_name=gitea) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","id","whoami"))) OR Processes.process="*hooks/post-index-change*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.process) as cmds from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where ((Processes.parent_process_name=git OR Processes.parent_process_name=gitea) AND (Processes.process_name IN ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","id","whoami"))) OR Processes.process="*hooks/post-index-change*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort - lastTime
Git server-side hook file written (hooks/post-index-change) - CVE-2026-60004 persistence AIInstallation High
Detects creation/modification of a hooks/post-index-change file (the exact CVE-2026-60004 payload path), or of other client-side hook names written by a git/gitea process into a repository hooks directory. post-index-change is an almost-never-used hook, so its appearance on a Gitea host is a strong exploit signal. Rationale: hooks/post-index-change is the verbatim payload path from the article ('An executable file placed at hooks/post-index-change ... lands in Git's hook directory and becomes active'); it is a rarely-used hook, and Gitea legitimately manages only pre-receive/post-receive/update server hooks (deliberately excluded), keeping this precise. Cross-checked against: • https://threats.wiz.io/all-techniques/misconfigured-gitea-abuse • https://www.rapid7.com/db/modules/exploit/multi/http/gitea_git_hooks_rce/
ATT&CKT1546 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer laptops (if MDE is on them) using Husky/pre-commit/lefthook, which write .git/hooks/pre-commit, post-merge, post-checkout - main FP for the non-post-index-change names
  • Legitimate Gitea repo provisioning writing standard server hooks (pre-receive/post-receive/update - excluded by design)
  • A DevOps admin manually installing a custom client hook in a checked-out working copy
  • Backup/restore of a repo directory re-creating existing hook files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has ".husky" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("husky","pre-commit","lefthook","node") and FolderPath !has "node_modules"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is a Gitea server (not a dev workstation) and read the hook file contents; a post-index-change hook on a server is almost always malicious. Check the writing process and account. 2) Contain: quarantine/remove the hook file, snapshot it for forensics, isolate the host if the file is non-empty/executable, and rotate Gitea service-account-reachable secrets. 3) Hunt: pivot to the diffpatch POSTs (UC1) that dropped it and to any shell it spawned (UC2); enumerate all repos on the instance for stray post-index-change/post-checkout hooks.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has "/hooks/"
| where FileName =~ "post-index-change"
    or (FileName in~ ("post-checkout","post-merge","post-commit","pre-commit") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("git","gitea"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has "/hooks/"
| where TargetFileName =~ "post-index-change"
    or (TargetFileName in~ ("post-checkout","post-merge","post-commit","pre-commit") and ActingProcessName has_any ("git","gitea"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Gitea version exposed to CVE-2026-60004 (pre-1.27.1) AIReconnaissance High
Vulnerability-management hunt surfacing hosts running Gitea affected by CVE-2026-60004 (versions 1.17 up to but not including the fixed 1.27.1). ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • TVM lag showing a host as vulnerable shortly after it was upgraded to 1.27.1
  • Air-gapped/internal-only Gitea instances flagged but not internet-reachable (lower priority, not a false match)
  • Containerised Gitea where the scanner reports the base image rather than the running binary version
  • Duplicate device records inflating the affected count
Suppression filter
| where SoftwareVersion !startswith "1.27.1"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is truly < 1.27.1 and whether the host is internet-facing and has open registration enabled. 2) Contain: schedule/apply the upgrade to 1.27.1; as interim mitigation disable open registration and/or the diffpatch route and restrict repo-write to trusted users. 3) Hunt: on every flagged host retro-run UC1/UC2/UC3 over the exposure window to confirm no pre-patch exploitation (stray post-index-change hooks, git-spawned shells).
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-60004"
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental

    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-

references:

author: Clankerusecase

tags:

    - attack.t1566.001

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'

    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:

            - '\wscript.exe'

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

Flying Eagle Android RAT Traces Found on 170 Servers as Source Code Circulates

The Hacker News
2026-07-29 11 use cases 4 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Source code for the Flying Eagle Android remote access trojan (RAT) framework is circulating through criminal Telegram channels. Hunt.io and independent researcher NetAskari traced matching control panels and certificates to 170 internet servers. They linked the framework to a fake "公安一网通办" Public Security service application targeting Android users in China. The kit supports payment-password

Flying Eagle Android RAT C2 / panel infrastructure callback (confirmed IOCs) AICommand & Control High
Hunts any monitored host (endpoint, proxy, firewall, DNS) resolving or connecting to the confirmed Flying Eagle SpyNote control-panel and distribution infrastructure named by Hunt.io and China's National Cybersecurity Notification Center. Fires on the specific C2 domains, distribution domains, and panel IPs — not a generic beaconing heuristic. Rationale: Every domain and IP is a confirmed IOC cross-verified in Hunt.io's report; 110gongan.com + 207.56.30.188 were additionally named in the China National Cybersecurity Notification Center's June 18 advisory. Distinct random subdomains (xyttkx.cc, j2x8a.top) make this near-zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/flying-eagle-android-rat-170-servers-night-dragon • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/flying-eagle-android-rat-traces-found.html • https://cybersecuritynews.com/a-leaked-android-rat/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1437.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or threat-intel analyst on the corporate network detonating/browsing the sample infrastructure
  • Automated URL/domain sandbox or crawler egressing through the monitored proxy
  • Shared-hosting IP reuse — 108.187.7.66/.71 (Antbox) or 154.44.25.12 later re-assigned to a benign tenant after the campaign
  • TI-platform connectors (MISP/OpenCTI) performing enrichment lookups against these indicators
  • A newly onboarded MDM/enrolled Android device beaconing that is already a known infection under IR
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe","MsMpEng.exe") and RemoteIP !in ("")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the internal host/device and the initiating process; if an Android/BYOD asset, confirm whether the '公安一网通办' / autoclicker_pro APK or any SpyNote sample is installed. 2) Contain: block all eight IPs and eight domains at proxy/firewall/DNS sink, isolate the device from the network and revoke any cached credentials/session tokens used from it. 3) Hunt: pivot on the src across DeviceNetworkEvents/DnsEvents for the other IOCs, check for the distribution-APK download (UC2) preceding the callback, and freeze/monitor any payment or banking accounts accessed from the device per the CNCERT advisory.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("110gongan.com","fusu.us.ci","fusu666.cc","ls.j2x8a.top","alcs.xyttkx.cc","txl.xyttkx.cc","h5.xyttkx.cc","s.orove.cn")
    or RemoteIP in ("207.56.30.188","207.56.30.194","108.187.7.66","108.187.7.71","77.105.161.235","154.44.25.12","85.137.253.48")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort,10) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by LastSeen desc
let iocDomains = dynamic(["110gongan.com","fusu.us.ci","fusu666.cc","ls.j2x8a.top","alcs.xyttkx.cc","txl.xyttkx.cc","h5.xyttkx.cc","s.orove.cn"]);
let iocIPs = dynamic(["207.56.30.188","207.56.30.194","108.187.7.66","108.187.7.71","77.105.161.235","154.44.25.12","85.137.253.48"]);
union
  (DnsEvents | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Name has_any (iocDomains) | project TimeGenerated, Src=ClientIP, Indicator=Name, IndType="DNS"),
  (CommonSecurityLog | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DestinationHostName has_any (iocDomains) or DestinationIP in (iocIPs) | project TimeGenerated, Src=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, DestinationIP), IndType="Firewall")

Flying Eagle / SpyNote malicious APK download by hash or distribution domain AIDelivery Medium
Detects a Flying Eagle builder-produced APK (SpyNote payload) landing on a monitored endpoint — matched by the confirmed sample SHA256 set or by an .apk file originating from the distribution domains 110gongan.com / fusu.us.ci. Targets the delivery step where a user sideloads the fake Public-Security app. Rationale: The seven SHA256 values are builder-generated SpyNote samples confirmed in Hunt.io's IOC table (autoclicker_pro.apk c692ad... is the actual 110gongan.com delivery APK). Hash match is deterministic; the .apk-from-distribution-domain arm catches repacked variants where the hash randomises. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/flying-eagle-android-rat-170-servers-night-dragon • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/flying-eagle-android-rat-traces-found.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1660
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst intentionally saving a sample APK to a sandbox/lab endpoint
  • MDM/EMM staging server hosting APKs for legitimate managed-app distribution (hash-arm won't fire, only the loose .apk-domain arm)
  • Mobile developer building/downloading in-house APKs to a Windows workstation
  • Security awareness team storing the IOC sample for phishing simulation
  • Threat-intel repo sync pulling the sample hash-set to a local malware zoo
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\MalwareLab\\","\\Samples\\","\\Detonation\\") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-sandbox","malware-analyst"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the SHA256 match vs the loose .apk arm; if hash-confirmed it is a definitive SpyNote sample — identify the downloading user, source URL, and referring email/message. 2) Contain: quarantine the file, block the source URL/domain, and if the APK reached an Android/BYOD device, isolate it and initiate mobile IR (uninstall, factory-consider, revoke tokens). 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/user against UC1 C2 callbacks and check email/web proxy for the 110gongan.com lure delivery; sweep all endpoints for the full hash-set.

    or (FileName endswith ".apk" and FileOriginUrl has_any ("110gongan.com","fusu.us.ci"))

Flying Eagle / SQLRCE / Night Dragon control-panel exposed on monitored web server AICommand & Control Medium
Threat-hunt for a Flying Eagle-family control panel (AdminPro / Ant-Design-Pro derived) running on any internally-monitored or reverse-proxied web server, identified by the campaign's distinctive login routes and HTTP 302→HTTPS redirect behaviour documented by Hunt.io. Surfaces a rogue/compromised server hosting the RAT panel. Rationale: Hunt.io explicitly documents the panel login routes /login?redirect=list/basic-list and /login?redirect=/basic plus the 302→HTTPS + Strict-Transport-Security fingerprint across the AdminPro, SQLRCE and Night Dragon variants; matching these routes on your own web/proxy logs finds a hosted panel. Defender has no IIS/web-access-log table so defender_kql is intentionally empty. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/flying-eagle-android-rat-170-servers-night-dragon
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ant Design Pro admin scaffold — 'list/basic-list' and '/basic' are default template routes and appear on benign in-house dashboards
  • Internal developer test/staging site built from the same Ant Design Pro starter
  • Vulnerability scanner or web crawler fuzzing /login?redirect= parameters
  • Pre-existing SSO portal that proxies a redirect= query parameter with similar values
Response runbook
1) Triage: fetch the flagged server's root page and TLS cert — confirm the AdminPro/SQLRCE/夜龙控制台 page title and the packaged cert (CN alcs.xyttkx.cc, SHA1 ab4224a6361e6f826fdb262276411e03f8177e30) to separate a real panel from a benign Ant Design Pro app. 2) Contain: if confirmed, isolate the server, preserve the nginx/PHP/MySQL/Node.js WebSocket stack for forensics, and block inbound access. 3) Hunt: enumerate connected victims from the panel's device list, pivot the server IP against UC1 IOCs, and check for the 中国龙.zip / Docker deployment artifacts on adjacent hosts.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csUriStem =~ "/login"
| where csUriQuery has_any ("redirect=list/basic-list","redirect=/basic")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count(), Clients=dcount(cIP), Statuses=make_set(scStatus,10) by Computer, sSiteName, csUriStem, csUriQuery
| order by LastSeen desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:

            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:

            - 'invoke-expression'

Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Install/import of compromised @joyfill 2773 beta package versions
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Node.js spawning shell/recon binaries or detached node -e loader · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Two Compromised joyfill npm Packages Run RAT When Imported Into Node.js
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Node.js modifying developer-tool modules for RAT self-reload persistence · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] RAT C2 egress to hardcoded joyfill IPs and /$/boot request paths · [LLM] Node.js resolving C2 via Tron + Binance Smart Chain dead-drop RPC · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Node.js spawning Python credential-stealer child · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Install/import of compromised @joyfill 2773 beta package versions AIDelivery High
Detects execution of npm/node referencing the hijacked @joyfill/components and @joyfill/layouts prerelease versions carrying the '2773' beta tag. These specific versions ship an obfuscated RAT that runs on import, so any host that installed or built against them must be treated as compromised. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete package names (@joyfill/components, @joyfill/layouts) and the unique '2773' beta tag common to all six malicious versions; the pairing is effectively zero-FP because no benign build references both tokens. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer intentionally auditing the malicious package in a sandbox VM
  • Internal mirror/proxy pre-fetch of the version for quarantine analysis
  • Security tooling that clones the tarball to diff it (StepSecurity-style research)
  • A package-lock file merge conflict resolution that lists the string in a diff view opened by node
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host actually resolved/built the 2773 version (check node_modules/@joyfill and package-lock.json), not just referenced it in a diff. 2) Contain: isolate the developer workstation and CI runner; the payload runs on import so treat the box as compromised — rotate all credentials present (browser, Git/GitHub CLI, keychains). 3) Hunt: pivot on the same DeviceName for outbound to the C2 IPs, node spawning python, and modification of @vscode/deviceid / GitHub Desktop main.js.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "joyfill" and ProcessCommandLine has "2773"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "joyfill" and CommandLine has "2773"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

RAT C2 egress to hardcoded joyfill IPs and /$/boot request paths AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections to the four command-and-control IPs and the distinctive HTTP request paths (/$/boot, /u/e, /u/f, /0x/js, /verify-human/, /snv) used by the joyfill RAT's Socket.IO channel and second-stage boot loader. High-fidelity IOC match. Rationale: Directly matches the article's four C2 IPs (incl. 23.27.13.43 that serves /$/boot) and the six unique request paths; these are singular IOCs with no benign use. Not externally cross-checked (article notes infra was likely taken down post-disclosure).
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/IOC validation scanners that deliberately probe the C2 IPs
  • A recycled/reassigned IP later hosting a benign service (IPs rotate)
  • Proxy logs replayed during a tabletop exercise
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a monitored subnet
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe or a detached node -e child) and confirm it correlates with a joyfill import on the same host. 2) Contain: block the four IPs at the perimeter, isolate the host, and pull the process for memory capture before reboot. 3) Hunt: sweep all egress logs org-wide for the same IPs/paths, and check for the blockchain resolver traffic (trongrid + bsc) that precedes the live-C2 resolution.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("/$/boot","/0x/js","/verify-human/","/u/e","/u/f","/snv")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP in ("166.88.134.62","23.27.13.43","198.105.127.210","23.27.202.27")
   or RequestURL has_any ("/$/boot","/0x/js","/verify-human/","/snv")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Node.js resolving C2 via Tron + Binance Smart Chain dead-drop RPC AICommand & Control Medium
Detects a node process contacting two or more public blockchain RPC endpoints (Tron, Aptos, BSC) used by the joyfill loader to resolve its live C2 through an on-chain transaction (eth_getTransactionByHash). A React/UI dev process reaching multiple chain RPCs is highly anomalous. Rationale: Ties the article's specific dead-drop resolver behaviour (Tron -> BSC via eth_getTransactionByHash) to the concrete RPC hosts; requiring >=2 distinct chain endpoints from a node process filters normal single-chain dApp traffic. Not externally cross-checked.
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate blockchain/web3 developer building a multi-chain dApp with node
  • Crypto wallet or exchange tooling that queries several RPC endpoints
  • node-based analytics service polling public chain data
  • CI job for a web3 project running integration tests against testnets
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "web3" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "hardhat" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "truffle"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host has no legitimate web3/blockchain project (check package.json deps and developer role); a UI/React shop hitting Tron+BSC is a strong TP. 2) Contain: isolate the host and capture the node process command line and memory; block the resolver domains if no legit web3 use. 3) Hunt: correlate the resolver window with subsequent egress to the hardcoded C2 IPs and /$/boot, and check for the python credential stealer child.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.trongrid.io","fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com","bsc-dataseed.binance.org","bsc-rpc.publicnode.com")
| summarize ChainEndpoints=make_set(RemoteUrl), Conns=count(), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where array_length(ChainEndpoints) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

| summarize ChainDomains=make_set(DnsQuery), Cnt=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by SrcIpAddr, DvcHostname, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where array_length(ChainDomains) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\node.exe OR *\Node.exe) @DestinationHostname:(api.trongrid.io OR fullnode.mainnet.aptoslabs.com OR bsc-dataseed.binance.org OR bsc-rpc.publicnode.com)

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=collect([DomainName]))
